issue_context.title: Make OrderedDictionaryKeyValueCollection implement IList
issue_context.body:
## [#15843 Ordered Dictionary keys are not numerically indexable](https://github.com/PowerShell/PowerShell/issues/15843)

Just to formalize a .Net request originated from a PowerShell issue (The impact is low and I do have several workarounds):

### Steps to reproduce

Indexing keys in a hash table does make much sense as the keys are unordered by design.
But are expected to work on an [`[ordered]`](https://docs.microsoft.com/powershell/module/microsoft.powershell.core/about/about_hash_tables#creating-ordered-dictionaries) dictionary.

```PowerShell
$a = [ordered]@{ a = 1; b = 2; c = 3 }
$a.Keys[0] # $a.get_Keys()[0]
$a.Keys[1] # $a.get_Keys()[1]
```





### Expected behavior

```console
# Index 0 return a
$a.Keys[0] # $a.get_Keys()[0]
a

# Index 1 return b
$a.Keys[1] # $a.get_Keys()[1]
b
```


### Actual behavior

```console
# Index 0 returns all keys
$a.Keys[0] # $a.get_Keys()[0]
a
b
c

# Index 1 and successive indices return $Null
$a.Keys[1] # $a.get_Keys()[1]
```


### Error details

```console
No errors (unless strict mode is set)
```

### Workarounds

```PowerShell
@($a.Keys)[0]

([object[]]$dict.Keys)[0]

$dict.Keys.ForEach{ $_ }[0]

$keys = [object[]]::new($dict.Keys.Count)
$dict.Keys.CopyTo($keys, 0)
$keys[0]
```

### Environment data

```powershell
Name                           Value
----                           -----
PSVersion                      7.1.3
PSEdition                      Core
GitCommitId                    7.1.3
OS                             Microsoft Windows 10.0.19042
Platform                       Win32NT
PSCompatibleVersions           {1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0…}
PSRemotingProtocolVersion      2.3
SerializationVersion           1.1.0.1
WSManStackVersion              3.0
```

### Suggested solution

Change the return type of `IDictionary.Keys` to `IList`
comments: This would be a significant [breaking change](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/main/docs/coding-guidelines/breaking-changes.md), i.e. any assembly that used this member would stop working on a newer version of the runtime. As such, I seriously doubt this change would be considered.

> This would be a significant [breaking change](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/main/docs/coding-guidelines/breaking-changes.md)

I was afraid of that and I am not able to oversee the impact here.
From my view (as a PowerShell scripter) the impact appears low. PowerShell is basically loosely language, the current implementation (returning a `OrderedDictionaryKeyValueCollection` type) is quite useless (in PowerShell). Besides, as PowerShell normally unrolls collections anyways, It probably won't break any existing PowerShell scripts. Meaning: all the given workarounds can be applied _multiple_ times on the `OrderedDictionaryKeyValueCollection` type without issue. In other words, all the given workarounds (all the known ways to enumerate the `OrderedDictionaryKeyValueCollection` type in PowerShell) will likely survive a fix.
But I understand that a program written in strict language as C# could simply break on a type definition or comparison.

I will leave it up to you to eventually close this issue as e.g. "**won't fix**" (or not).

> PowerShell is basically loosely language, the current implementation (returning a `OrderedDictionaryKeyValueCollection` type) is quite useless (in PowerShell).

I'm not too familiar with PS, but would changing just the implementation, by making `OrderedDictionaryKeyValueCollection` implement `IList` help? Because that wouldn't be a breaking change at all, and so should have a much better chance of being accepted.

@SeeminglyScience, sorry for reaching out to you...
Can you confirm that making `OrderedDictionaryKeyValueCollection` implement `IList` fixes the issue in PowerShell?

Changing the return type of `IDictionary.Keys` would make every existing compiled .NET program (C#, F#, VB, etc) that used it fail with a MissingMethodException (generally when the calling method gets JITted).  It's pretty much a "nope, not gonna happen".

It looks like OrderedDictionaryKeyValueCollection could be an IList without too much effort.  That would help in certain cases (such as the System.Linq.Enumerable methods) that do a runtime type check to opportunistically do things a faster way.  Don't know if it would have any impact on PowerShell usage, though.

> @SeeminglyScience, sorry for reaching out to you...
> Can you confirm that making `OrderedDictionaryKeyValueCollection` implement `IList` fixes the issue in PowerShell?

Yep that would enable indexing in PowerShell

This issue has been marked with the `api-needs-work` label. This may suggest that the proposal requires further refinement before it can be considered for API review. Please refer to our [API review guidelines](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/main/docs/project/api-review-process.md) for a detailed description of the process. 

When ready to submit an amended proposal, please ensure that the original post in this issue has been updated, following the API proposal template and examples as provided in the guidelines.

> I presume that your ask is not limited to `OrderedDictionary` but you would probably want to see this in all sorted dictionary implementations?

The `System.Collections.Specialized.OrderedDictionary` is most used in _specialized_ collection in PowerShell (as it is accelerated with `[Ordered]`) but not limited to it.
So, **yes**, it would be nice to have this on all other specialized collection key lists as well.
This would simplify the PowerShell syntax from e.g.  `@($Dictionary.Keys)[0]` to `$Dictionary.Keys[0]`.
Thanks. I wonder if we could get feedback from the pwsh team on what other sorted dictionaries might benefit from this. cc @SteveL-MSFT

As  PowerShell is capable of using any .Net (sorted) dictionary, like:

```PowerShell
$Sorted = [System.Collections.Generic.SortedDictionary[String,Int]]::New()
$Sorted.Add('b', 2)
$Sorted.Add('a', 1)
@($Sorted.Keys)[1] # Expected improvement: $Sorted.Keys[1]
b
```
I am pretty sure that any .net (sorted) dictionary would benefit from a key list with an explicit IList Interface implementation but I don't have the resource to test whether it works as expected.
